title: When should you use WebSocket vs SSE: WebSocket for chat, gaming, collaborative editing (need two-way); SSE for live notifications, stock tickers, dashboards (server→client only, simpler, auto-reconnect)?
shortTitle: When should you use WebSocket vs SSE
keyPoints: WebSocket is full-duplex: both client and server send messages independently after the upgrade handshake.
SSE is half-duplex: the server streams events to the client, and the client cannot send on the same channel.
SSE runs over plain HTTP, passes through proxies, and the browser's EventSource auto-reconnects with last-event-id resume.
WebSocket needs WebSocket-aware infrastructure, manual reconnection, and manual heartbeats.
Default to SSE when the flow is server-push only; reach for WebSocket only when real-time client-to-server messaging is needed.
In banking, notifications and tickers are SSE; trading terminals and support chat are WebSocket.

s1_definition.oneliner: Use WebSocket when the client must send data back in real time (chat, gaming, trading); use SSE when the server only pushes to the client (notifications, tickers, dashboards), because SSE is simpler and auto-reconnects.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **WebSocket** – full-duplex, two-way communication over a single upgraded TCP connection; suited to interactive scenarios like chat, gaming, and collaborative editing.
- **SSE (Server-Sent Events)** – one-way server-to-client streaming over a single long-lived HTTP connection with built-in automatic reconnection; suited to notifications, tickers, and dashboards.
- **Decision rule** – default to SSE when the flow is purely server-push; reach for WebSocket only when real-time client-to-server messaging is genuinely needed.
- **Occasional client action** – if a mostly-one-way feature needs the client to act (e.g. acknowledge an alert), make that action a normal REST POST alongside the SSE stream.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a trader and the market-data desk need a two-way phone line where both shout simultaneously: that is WebSocket. The stock price board broadcasts to everyone watching: one-way, and if someone steps out and comes back the board is still showing: that is SSE. If all you need is to broadcast, the one-way loudspeaker is simpler and self-healing.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Decision Rule:

  Does the client need to send data back in real time?
  ├── YES → WebSocket
  │         (chat, trading, collaboration)
  │
  └── NO  → SSE
            (notifications, tickers, dashboards)
            If occasional client action needed:
            use a separate REST POST alongside SSE

  SSE:       Client ←──events──── Server   (auto-reconnect)
  WebSocket: Client ←──messages──→ Server  (manual reconnect)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
WebSocket and SSE are both persistent-connection real-time techniques that differ in direction and complexity. WebSocket is full-duplex: after the upgrade handshake, both client and server send messages independently, which suits genuinely interactive two-way scenarios like chat, collaborative editing, and a trading terminal. SSE is one-way: the server streams events to the client over a single HTTP connection, which suits server-push-only scenarios like notifications, tickers, and dashboards.

The practical advantage of SSE when one-way suffices is significant. It runs over plain HTTP, passes through proxies and firewalls that sometimes block WebSocket upgrades, and the browser's EventSource reconnects automatically and resumes from the last event ID. WebSocket requires WebSocket-aware infrastructure, manual reconnection, manual heartbeats, and loses HTTP caching.

At National Bank of India, payment notifications and the stock-price ticker are one-way, so they run on SSE with automatic reconnection. The active trading terminal genuinely needs two-way messaging, so it uses WebSocket. When the notification feature needed client acknowledgment, the team did not complicate the SSE stream: the acknowledgment is a plain REST POST alongside the one-way stream.

The decision rule is simple: if the client must push in real time, use WebSocket; otherwise use SSE. If a mostly-one-way feature needs an occasional client action, make that action a REST call.

Remember one sentence: default to SSE for server push because it is simpler and self-healing; reach for WebSocket only when the client must talk back in real time.
